sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: the unposted speed ladder, white versus orange signs, sign shapes, school-zone speeds and railroad stops
Look-alike numbers and shapes from the speed and sign pages, each tied to one handbook page; hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec11-R01 | anchor: A01
Open highways and city freeways default to 55 mph, designated open highways to 65 mph, and rural freeways to 75 mph. [A01]
Why it matters: group speed limits; difficulty three; confusable sec11-F04 versus sec11-F05.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-R02 | anchor: A01
A school crosswalk approach defaults to 15 mph, while a business or residential district defaults to 25 mph. [A01]
Why it matters: group speed limits; difficulty two; confusable sec11-F02 versus sec11-F03.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-R03 | anchor: A01
A white sign with black letters is the legal maximum, while an orange sign with black letters is only a recommended safe speed for that spot. [A01]
Why it matters: group speed signs; difficulty two; confusable sec11-F07 versus sec11-F08.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-R04 | anchor: A01
Bad weather calls for both a lower speed and twice the usual following distance, not just one of them. [A01]
Why it matters: group conditions; difficulty two; prereq sec11-F11.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-R05 | anchor: A02
An octagon always means stop, while a triangle means yield to cross or merging traffic. [A02]
Why it matters: group sign shapes; difficulty one; confusable sec11-F17 versus sec11-F18.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec11-R06 | anchor: A02
A pennant marks the start of a no-passing zone, while a yellow diamond warns of a possible hazard ahead. [A02]
Why it matters: group sign shapes; difficulty two; confusable sec11-F22 versus sec11-F23.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec11-R07 | anchor: A02
The small yellow square that may sit under a curve sign is the one that shows the safe speed through that curve, while the curve sign itself only warns of the bend. [A02]
Why it matters: group speed signs; difficulty two; prereq sec11-F21.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec11-R08 | anchor: A03
A pentagon is the school crossing shape, while a circle is the railroad warning shape. [A03]
Why it matters: group sign shapes; difficulty two; confusable sec11-F24 versus sec11-F30.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-R09 | anchor: A03
The school-zone limit of 15 mph runs from the first portable sign until past the crossing sign, and it lapses when those portable signs are removed. [A03]
Why it matters: group school zones; difficulty three; confusable sec11-F26 versus sec11-F27.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-R10 | anchor: A03
At a railroad crossing, any one of flashing red lights, a lowered barricade, ringing bells or a flagger is enough to require stopping at least 15 feet from the nearest rail. [A03]
Why it matters: group railroad crossings; difficulty three; prereq sec11-F32.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-R11 | anchor: A03
The school crossing speed and the railroad stopping distance share the number fifteen but measure different things, miles per hour versus feet. [A03]
Why it matters: group numbers; difficulty three; confusable sec11-F26 versus sec11-F32.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-R12 | anchor: A03
If a vehicle stalls on the tracks, the rule the manual gives is simply to get out of it. [A03]
Why it matters: group railroad crossings; difficulty one; prereq sec11-F37.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]
